warmup.q: A Quarkus 3.40 endpoint returns Uni<Parcel> and builds it with Uni.createFrom().item(repository.findById(id)), where findById calls a database the blocking way. Which thread runs that database call?
options: A worker thread, because Quarkus sees the database call
A Vert.x event loop (IO thread), because the method returns Uni
A virtual thread, because Quarkus 3.40 runs everything on virtual threads
The Mutiny scheduler, because Uni is lazy
warmup.why: Quarkus REST picks the thread from the signature: Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher and Kotlin suspend mean "non-blocking", so the method runs on the IO thread. findById runs while the method builds the Uni, so the database call blocks an event loop. Quarkus can't see inside your method; add @Blocking or return a plain value.

opening:
Picture a company that runs post offices. Every branch puts last lesson's clerks at the counter, and the company gives each branch a rule book for jobs. The rule book reads only the label on each job ticket. A job marked "quick" stays with the counter clerk. An unmarked job goes to the back office, which has a fixed number of workers. A job stamped "helper" gets a temporary helper, hired for that one job, who costs almost nothing while the job waits.

That company is Quarkus, a Java framework for web services that runs its counter on Vert.x. The surprise is how literally it reads the labels. It never looks at the job itself.

So the trap is a relabeled ticket. Mark a slow database job "quick", perhaps in the hope of speeding it up, and the counter clerk takes it while the whole queue waits. In Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule, we sent slow jobs to the back office by hand. In this lesson, we'll read Quarkus's labels, change them, block a counter clerk with Quarkus's settings, and hire temporary helpers. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a company rule book that reads only the label on each job ticket. Quarkus works the same way: the return type and three annotations pick the counter clerk, the back office or a temporary helper, and Quarkus never looks inside the method.

Now search your own endpoints for a Uni return or a suspend fun that calls a blocking repository, client or library. Each one is a slow job wearing a "quick" label.

Next, we'll meet Jetty 12, a server with its own doormen, light-watchers and pool of clerks. How does it decide, task by task, who serves each customer?

sections.h: The label on the ticket: how Quarkus picks a thread from the return type
sections.html:
Quarkus is a framework for web services: programs that answer requests sent over HTTP, the protocol behind web pages. Its HTTP layer is a Vert.x server, so every request is first read on a Vert.x event loop, which Quarkus calls an IO thread. That's the counter clerk. Everything in this lesson is pinned to Quarkus 3.40.

Quarkus REST, its library for writing web endpoints (formerly called RESTEasy Reactive), then decides who runs your code. An endpoint is a Java method that answers one kind of request, such as GET /prices/P-17. Annotations, the labels that start with @, tell Quarkus which requests it answers. The Quarkus reactive architecture guide describes the choice that follows. Quarkus calls your code right there on the IO thread, which saves a thread switch, or on a worker thread. A worker thread comes from a bounded pool, and it is allowed to block.

The decision comes from the method's signature: the label on the ticket. A method that returns Uni, Multi, CompletionStage or Publisher, or a Kotlin suspend function, counts as non-blocking and runs on the IO thread. All of these say "the answer comes later". Uni, from the Mutiny library that Quarkus uses, holds one result, and Multi holds a stream of them. CompletionStage is the JDK's own future, Publisher is the Reactive Streams standard's type for a stream of results, and a suspend function can pause without holding its thread. Anything else, such as a method that returns a Price directly, runs on a worker thread.

Here is the price desk as a Quarkus service, with one endpoint of each kind:

Java
@Path("/prices")
public class PriceResource {
    @Inject PriceBook priceBook;              // a database, called the blocking way
    @Inject LivePrices livePrices;            // a non-blocking client that returns Uni

    @GET @Path("/{parcel}")
    public Price price(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) {        // plain value: worker thread
        return priceBook.find(parcel);
    }

    @GET @Path("/{parcel}/live")
    public Uni<Price> live(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) {    // Uni: IO thread
        return livePrices.find(parcel);
    }
}
Kotlin
@Path("/prices")
class PriceResource(
    private val priceBook: PriceBook,         // a database, called the blocking way
    private val livePrices: LivePrices,       // a non-blocking client that returns Uni
) {
    @GET @Path("/{parcel}")
    fun price(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Price =         // plain value: worker thread
        priceBook.find(parcel)

    @GET @Path("/{parcel}/live")
    suspend fun live(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Price =  // suspend: IO thread
        livePrices.find(parcel).awaitSuspending()
}

@Inject asks Quarkus to hand the class the objects it needs; in Kotlin, the constructor does the same job. The first endpoint returns a plain Price, so Quarkus sends it to the back office. The second promises a result later, so it stays at the counter.

Read the rule as a promise you make. A Uni return type tells Quarkus "this method won't block", so Quarkus skips the hop to a worker and saves its cost. Quarkus believes that promise completely, and never looks inside the method. Break it with a database call inside, and you're back in lesson 5, with every other connection on that event loop waiting.

Here the ticket picture breaks. A real clerk would notice a forty-minute job marked "quick". Quarkus never will.

The back office is a bounded pool, like the ones in the executors track. Its size, quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads, defaults to the larger of 8 × CPUs and 200 in 3.40: 200 threads on a 4-core machine.

The return type is a promise about blocking, and Quarkus believes it. Return Uni only from code that never waits.

When the signature tells the wrong story, you can change the label.

sections.h: Changing the label: @Blocking, @NonBlocking, and the @Transactional disagreement
sections.html:
Changing the label takes one annotation. @Blocking (from io.smallrye.common.annotation) sends a method to a worker even if it returns Uni. @NonBlocking keeps a method on the IO thread even if it returns a plain value. Both work on a method, on a class, or on your jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass, the class that stands for the whole service, which sets the default for all of it. Filters, small pieces of code that run before or after every endpoint, follow their endpoint: under @Blocking they run on the worker, otherwise on the IO thread.

Java
@Blocking                                          // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker
@GET @Path("/{parcel}/archive")
public Uni<Price> archived(@PathParam("parcel") String parcel) {
    return Uni.createFrom().item(priceBook.find(parcel));   // the database call runs right here
}
Kotlin
@Blocking                                          // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker
@GET @Path("/{parcel}/archive")
fun archived(@PathParam("parcel") parcel: String): Uni<Price> =
    Uni.createFrom().item(priceBook.find(parcel))  // the database call runs right here

Look at the line inside. Uni.createFrom().item(...) wraps a value that already exists, so priceBook.find(parcel) runs while the method builds the Uni, on whatever thread runs the method. Without @Blocking, that's the counter clerk.

Transactions are where the rule book argues with itself. A transaction groups several database changes so that they all happen or none do. JTA, the Jakarta Transactions API, is Java's standard way to run one, and you ask for it with @Transactional. JTA blocks the thread that uses it.

The Quarkus REST guide as released with 3.40.1 says a method or class annotated with jakarta.transaction.Transactional "will also be treated as a blocking method", and that an explicit @Blocking or @NonBlocking overrides this. The same guide on Quarkus's main branch, its newest code, says the opposite. Since 3.35, it says, @Transactional no longer makes a method blocking, the return type decides, and a Uni method that uses JTA needs an explicit @Blocking. The research for this track couldn't find the code that settles which is right for 3.40.

So don't depend on either reading. Put @Blocking on every endpoint that uses JTA and doesn't return a plain value. It costs nothing when the rule already applies and saves you when it doesn't.

When it doesn't, at least the failure is loud. Quarkus's JTA support comes from a library called Narayana, and its interceptor, the code that runs around a @Transactional method, checks whether blocking is allowed before it starts a transaction. In 3.40.1, on an IO thread, it throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException: "@Transactional cannot start a JTA transaction within a reactive pipeline. If the annotated method is intended to be blocking, ensure it is executed on a worker thread, for example by annotating it with @Blocking. ..."

When the signature tells the wrong story, change the label. On a @Transactional endpoint that returns Uni, write @Blocking.

That exception is one way Quarkus catches a blocked counter clerk. Lesson 5's floor manager is the other, and Quarkus gives him new instructions.

try.title: Read the rules both ways
steps: Take @Transactional public Uni<Void> record(Parcel p). Where does it run under the 3.40.1 docs? Under the main-branch docs? What does the JTA interceptor do in each case?
Now take @Transactional @NonBlocking public Uni<Void> record(Parcel p). Where does it run, and what happens?
Check the first answer against the lab test that mentions @Transactional.
try.expect: Under the 3.40.1 docs the first method runs on a worker, and the transaction starts normally. Under the main-branch rule it runs on the IO thread, and the interceptor throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException before your code runs. The second method runs on the IO thread under both readings, because an explicit annotation wins, so it always throws. In every case @Blocking would have given the same working result, which is why it belongs on the method.

sections.h: When a counter clerk blocks: Quarkus's settings and its fast failures
sections.html:
Quarkus configures its Vert.x differently from plain Vert.x, and the differences change what your logs show:

Setting Plain Vert.x 5 Quarkus 3.40
event loops 2 × CPUs CPUs, at least 2, at most one per 10 MB of max heap (the memory for objects)
warn about a blocked loop after 2 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.max-event-loop-execute-time)
include the stack trace after 5 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time)
threads for blocking work worker pool: 20 quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads: max(8 × CPUs, 200)

A comment in Quarkus's source explains the first row. Twice the number of cores used to be the recommendation, but matching cores one to one seemed more reasonable, and it saves memory. On a 4-core laptop that means 4 event loops instead of 8, so one blocked loop stalls a quarter of your connections instead of an eighth.

The third row is the friendly difference. QuarkusLikeLoopDemo builds a plain Vert.x instance with Quarkus's settings and blocks an event loop for 3 seconds. The first warning already carries the stack trace:

plain Vert.x default event loops: 8, Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(3420 MB / 10, 4 cpus)) = 4
[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2681 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked
	at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509)
	at workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.lambda$main$0(QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java:30)

In the post office, Quarkus's floor manager writes down what the clerk is doing on his very first pass. In a real Quarkus service the line goes through Quarkus's own logging, so the prefix differs, but the message and the stack are Vert.x's. The first frame below Thread.sleep is your endpoint.

Some Quarkus APIs don't wait for the floor manager at all. They check where they run and fail at once with BlockingOperationNotAllowedException, which extends IllegalStateException. The JTA interceptor from the previous section is one. Reading a request body as a blocking stream on the IO thread is another, and it fails with "Attempting a blocking read on io thread".

Go one level down, and the check is simple. Quarkus asks its IO-thread detectors whether the current thread is an IO thread, and the Vert.x detector in 3.40.1 returns Context.isOnEventLoopThread(), the same call this lesson's lab uses. A fast exception in a test is a better way to find a blocking call than a slow event loop in production.

Quarkus reports a blocked IO thread after 2 seconds, stack and all. Read the first frame of your own code below the block.

Warnings and exceptions tell you a counter clerk blocked. The last label in the rule book avoids the back office's limit altogether.

try.title: Block an IO thread with Quarkus settings
steps: Open QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict the event-loop count it computes for your machine.
Predict whether the first blocked-thread warning comes with a stack trace. Run it.
Run it again with -Pargs=1500. How many warnings now, and why?

code.title: QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ public class QuarkusLikeLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long sleepMs = args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 3_000; int cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); long maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024); int quarkusLoops = (int) Math.max(2, Math.min(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus)); // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads System.out.println("plain Vert.x default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + ", Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(" + maxHeapMb + " MB / 10, " + cpus + " cpus)) = " + quarkusLoops); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext(v -> { System.out.println("[endpoint] on " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ", Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=" + Context.isOnEventLoopThread()); try { Thread.sleep(sleepMs); // a database call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }); Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } }

alt.title: QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Context import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val sleepMs = args.getOrNull(0)?.toLong() ?: 3_000L val cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024) val quarkusLoops = maxOf(2L, minOf(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus.toLong())).toInt() // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads println("plain Vert.x default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE}, " + "Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min($maxHeapMb MB / 10, $cpus cpus)) = $quarkusLoops") val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)) // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext { println("[endpoint] on ${Thread.currentThread().name}, Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=${Context.isOnEventLoopThread()}") Thread.sleep(sleepMs) // a database call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() }

try.expect: With a few gigabytes of max heap the memory cap doesn't bite, so the count equals your CPUs (4 here, against Vert.x's 8). The first warning, between 2 and 3 seconds in, already includes VertxException: Thread blocked and the stack, because the warning-exception time is 2 s. With a 1,500 ms block there is no warning at all: the checker only reports a task that has run longer than 2 seconds, so short blocks stay out of the logs.

sections.h: Temporary helpers: @RunOnVirtualThread without the worker-pool cap
sections.html:
The back office has a fixed number of workers. @RunOnVirtualThread is the third label in the rule book: it tells Quarkus to run the method on a new virtual thread, instead of the IO thread or a worker. A virtual thread is a thread the JDK manages itself. It runs on a carrier, an ordinary operating system thread, and while it waits it hands the carrier back, so a waiting virtual thread costs a few kilobytes of memory. In the post office, it's the temporary helper, hired for one job, who sits down while the job waits.

The code stays blocking style. A database call, or uni.await().atMost(...) on a Mutiny Uni, parks the virtual thread, and the JDK wakes it when the result is ready. VirtualVsWorkerDemo shows what the back office's size costs. 200 requests arrive on one IO context, and each makes a 100 ms blocking call:

worker pool (20 threads)   200 calls x 100 ms -> 1,037 ms on 20 distinct threads
virtual thread per call    200 calls x 100 ms ->   113 ms on 200 distinct threads

Twenty workers needed ten rounds of 100 ms: Little's law from lesson 1, 20 threads / 0.1 s = 200 calls a second. Two hundred helpers needed one. The Quarkus virtual threads guide compares the three models in one table, and its costs column is the part to remember:

Model Runs on Main cost
plain return value worker thread the pool caps concurrency
Uni and friends IO thread more complex code
@RunOnVirtualThread a new virtual thread pinning, monopolization, inefficient object pooling

Pinning means a virtual thread that can't hand its carrier back while it waits. On Java 21 to 23 that happens when it blocks inside synchronized. JDK 24 removed that case (JEP 491), but native code, code written in C and called from Java, can still pin, and the guide notes that the PostgreSQL driver pgjdbc before 42.6.0 pins often on 21 to 23. Monopolization means CPU-heavy work that never blocks, so it never hands the carrier back: virtual threads are for work that waits, not work that computes. And libraries such as Jackson (which reads and writes JSON) and Netty keep pools of objects per thread, assuming a few long-lived threads. A new virtual thread per request defeats those pools.

Two more things stay true. Helpers don't limit anything. 200 virtual threads sharing a 20-connection database pool still queue at the pool, so put a semaphore (a counter of permits that makes extra callers wait) or the pool's own limit in front of anything fragile. And the request still arrives on an IO thread. @RunOnVirtualThread works by moving your code off it.

A virtual thread per request removes the back office's cap, and with it the back office's protection. Put the limit back in front of the database.

try.title: Pool cap versus virtual threads
steps: Open VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict both times before running.
Give the worker pool 40 threads: change Vertx.vertx() to Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setWorkerPoolSize(40)). Predict the new worker time, then run.

code.title: VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.Promise; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ public class VirtualVsWorkerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); // default worker pool: 20 threads Context server = vertx.getOrCreateContext(); // where the requests arrive Thread.Builder virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0); // used only on the server's thread for (boolean virtual : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Future<Object>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { Promise<Object> done = Promise.promise(); server.runOnContext(v -> { Runnable blockingCall = () -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); try { Thread.sleep(100); // a database, a slow web service... } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } done.complete(); }; if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall); // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(() -> { blockingCall.run(); return null; }, false); // like @Blocking }); calls.add(done.future()); } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads%n", virtual ? "virtual thread per call" : "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size()); } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } }

alt.title: VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.Promise import io.vertx.core.Vertx import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ fun main() { val vertx = Vertx.vertx() // default worker pool: 20 threads val server = vertx.getOrCreateContext() // where the requests arrive val virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0) // used only on the server's thread for (virtual in listOf(false, true)) { val threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(200) { val done = Promise.promise<Any>() server.runOnContext { val blockingCall = Runnable { threads += Thread.currentThread().name Thread.sleep(100) // a database, a slow web service... done.complete() } if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall) // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Any> { blockingCall.run(); "" }, false) // like @Blocking } done.future() } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads".format( if (virtual) "virtual thread per call" else "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size)) } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() }

try.expect: About 1,000 ms on 20 worker threads (200 calls / 20 threads x 100 ms) and about 110 to 130 ms on 200 virtual threads; later runs for this lesson measured 1,059 and 132 ms. With 40 workers it drops to about 500 to 600 ms (534 and 598 ms in earlier runs): Little's law again, throughput = threads / time per call. The virtual version has no such cap, which is its strength, and also why you add your own limit in front of a fragile service.

compare.title: The lab's dispatch rules in Kotlin and Java

java.title: DispatchRules.java
java.html: final class DispatchRules { private static final Set<ReturnKind> NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS = EnumSet.of( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND); static Target target(Endpoint e) { Set<Marker> m = e.markers(); if (m.contains(Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD)) return Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.BLOCKING)) return Target.WORKER; if (m.contains(Marker.NON_BLOCKING)) return Target.IO_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.TRANSACTIONAL)) return Target.WORKER; return NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS.contains(e.returns()) ? Target.IO_THREAD : Target.WORKER; } }

kotlin.title: DispatchRules.kt
kotlin.html: object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } }

compare.note: Both encode the same first-match-wins rules; Kotlin's when without a subject reads like the figure, and Java uses early returns. The language difference that matters is in Quarkus itself. Java has no suspend, so a Java endpoint is non-blocking only through its return type, while a Kotlin suspend fun with a plain return type is non-blocking too, and runs on the IO thread. One Kotlin trap from this lesson's lab: Vert.x 5's Future has a member await(), and in Kotlin a member always wins over an extension with the same name, so a test helper fun <T> Future<T>.await() is silently ignored. The lab's test calls its helper awaitResult() for that reason.

worked.title: Pick the thread for four post office endpoints

steps.say: A tracking lookup reads the parcel from a database the blocking way. Plain return type, so it runs on a worker. Nothing to add.
steps.code: @GET @Path("/parcels/{id}") public Parcel byId(@PathParam("id") String id) { // worker thread return parcels.findById(id); // blocking database call }

alt.html: @GET @Path("/parcels/{id}") fun byId(@PathParam("id") id: String): Parcel = // worker thread parcels.findById(id) // blocking database call

steps.say: A label-printing endpoint records the label in a JTA transaction and returns Uni because a client library wants one. Under the 3.40.1 docs @Transactional alone would send it to a worker; under the main-branch docs it would run on the IO thread, and the interceptor would throw. Add @Blocking, and both readings agree.
steps.code: @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/parcels/{id}/label") public Uni<Label> printLabel(@PathParam("id") String id) { return Uni.createFrom().item(labels.print(id)); // database writes inside a JTA transaction }

alt.html: @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/parcels/{id}/label") fun printLabel(@PathParam("id") id: String): Uni<Label> = Uni.createFrom().item(labels.print(id)) // database writes inside a JTA transaction

steps.say: A live feed of parcel scans comes from a non-blocking client and never waits. Multi keeps it on the IO thread with no thread switch, which is the case the reactive model is built for.
steps.code: @GET @Path("/scans") public Multi<Scan> scans() { // IO thread return scanFeed.subscribe(); // non-blocking source }

alt.html: @GET @Path("/scans") fun scans(): Multi<Scan> = // IO thread scanFeed.subscribe() // non-blocking source

steps.say: A customs report calls a slow outside web service (2 s) that accepts at most 50 calls at once, and the customs office sends bursts of hundreds of requests. The worker pool would cap the throughput, so give each request a virtual thread, and put the outside service's limit back with a semaphore.
steps.code: private final Semaphore customsSlots = new Semaphore(50); @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/customs/{day}") public Report customs(@PathParam("day") String day) throws InterruptedException { customsSlots.acquire(); // 1. respect the outside service's limit try { return customsClient.reportFor(day); // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { customsSlots.release(); } }

alt.html: private val customsSlots = Semaphore(50) @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/customs/{day}") fun customs(@PathParam("day") day: String): Report { customsSlots.acquire() // 1. respect the outside service's limit try { return customsClient.reportFor(day) // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { customsSlots.release() } }

lab.title: Simulate Quarkus's rule book on plain Vert.x
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail with NotImplementedError. Read Endpoint.kt for the types: an endpoint has a name, a return kind and a set of markers (the annotations).
Write DispatchRules.target with a when that applies the four rules in its KDoc, first match wins. The four rule tests should pass.
Write BlockingGuard.check: throw BlockingNotAllowedException("Attempting $what on an IO thread") when Context.isOnEventLoopThread() is true.

Write Dispatcher.invoke: receive the request with server.runOnContext { ... }, then run the body there (IO thread), through vertx.executeBlocking(callable, false) (worker) or on a new virtual thread, and complete a Promise with the result or the failure.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then change false to the default and see which test fails, and why.
hints: Marker.BLOCKING in endpoint.markers reads naturally in Kotlin.
val p = Promise.promise<T>(), then p.complete(value) or p.fail(e), and return p.future(). For the worker branch, vertx.executeBlocking(task, false).onComplete(p) passes the result straight on.
Give the Callable an explicit type (val task: Callable<T> = Callable { body() }); Kotlin can fail to infer Vert.x types whose @Nullable annotation lives in vertx-codegen.
Every request goes through the one server context, so an ordered executeBlocking would make the four 300 ms calls queue: that is what the overlap test catches.

drill.title: Write the rule book from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a function that takes an endpoint's return kind and its annotations and returns IO_THREAD, WORKER or VIRTUAL_THREAD, using Quarkus 3.40's documented rules. For which rule would you add @Blocking anyway, to stay safe on any 3.x version?

answer.html: object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } } // add @Blocking to @Transactional endpoints that return Uni (or are suspend): // the 3.40.1 and main-branch docs disagree about the TRANSACTIONAL rule.

recap: Every Quarkus request arrives on an IO thread, a Vert.x event loop. Quarkus REST then reads the signature: Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher and Kotlin suspend stay on the IO thread, and plain return values go to a worker.
@Blocking and @NonBlocking override the signature on a method, a class or the Application.
The 3.40.1 docs say @Transactional makes a method blocking, and the main-branch docs say it no longer does. Put @Blocking on JTA endpoints that return Uni either way.
Quarkus 3.40 runs one event loop per CPU (at least 2), warns after 2 s and prints the stack at 2 s. Guarded APIs throw BlockingOperationNotAllowedException on an IO thread.
@RunOnVirtualThread runs blocking code on a new virtual thread with no pool cap; watch for pinning, CPU-heavy work and per-thread object pools.
The limit: Quarkus trusts the label and never looks inside the method, and virtual threads limit nothing. Honest labels and a limit in front of the database stay your job.

explain.prompt: A teammate changed a database endpoint to return Uni "to make it reactive", and latency got worse under load. Explain what Quarkus 3.40 does with that endpoint and what they should do instead.
explain.answer: Quarkus REST decides the thread from the signature, like a rule book that reads only the label on a job. A Uni return type means the method promises not to block, so Quarkus runs it on the IO thread, a Vert.x event loop, without switching to a worker. Wrapping a blocking database call in Uni.createFrom().item(...) runs the call while the method builds the Uni, so the call blocks the event loop and every other connection on it waits. Before the change, the plain return type put the call on a worker thread, which protected the event loop. They should go back to a plain return type, or add @Blocking if they must return Uni, or switch to a non-blocking database client so the method really doesn't block. If the reason for the change was the worker pool's limit, @RunOnVirtualThread with a limit on database calls is another option.

deeper.html:
A few details from the Quarkus 3.40 sources and docs help when you debug thread choices.

Filters follow their endpoint. A @ServerRequestFilter runs on the worker for a @Blocking endpoint and on the IO thread otherwise, so a filter that does a blocking lookup (say, checking a key against a database) blocks the event loop for every non-blocking endpoint. @ServerRequestFilter(nonBlocking = true) forces a filter onto the IO thread, which is only safe if it really never blocks.

To check which thread runs your code, log Thread.currentThread().getName() or assert io.vertx.core.Context.isOnEventLoopThread() in a @QuarkusTest, Quarkus's annotation for tests that start the whole service. Event-loop threads are named vert.x-eventloop-thread-N, and Quarkus's worker threads usually have executor-thread in their names.

The Vert.x settings live under quarkus.vertx.*: event-loops-pool-size, max-event-loop-execute-time, warning-exception-time and max-worker-execute-time (60 s). The old quarkus.vertx.worker-pool-size is deprecated in favor of quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads. Raising the event-loop count rarely helps a service that blocks: it only spreads the damage over more loops. Removing the blocking call is the fix.

Finally, a version note on the @Transactional disagreement: the 3.40.1-tagged guide and the main-branch guide were both read for this track, and the code that applies the rule was not found. If you need certainty for your exact Quarkus version, write a @QuarkusTest that calls a @Transactional endpoint returning Uni and asserts which thread it ran on.
